title: EXPLAINER: What is the South China Sea Code of Conduct?
summary: The long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) has yet to be completed with Beijing and member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) unable to agree on several issues…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 6:04pm

The long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) has yet to be completed with Beijing and member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) unable to agree on several issues — but what is it? And what is taking so long for the involved nations to agree?

While conflict in the South China Sea has had tense confrontations between China and the Philippines, parts of the contested waters have other claimants, including Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, and Brunei.

According to the ASEAN's website, member state parties and Beijing agreed to issue the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) in 2002 to maintain peace in the disputed waters.

The agreement stated that all parties are seeking peaceful resolutions to their maritime disputes to ensure regional stability. In 2011, the Guidelines for the Implementation of the DOC was established, which further reinforced the declaration.

"The Parties concerned undertake to resolve their territorial and jurisdictional disputes by peaceful means, without resorting to the threat or use of force, through friendly consultations and negotiations by sovereign states directly concerned, in accordance with universally recognized principles of international law, including the 1982 UN (United Nations) Convention on the Law of the Sea," the DOC read, referring to the UNCLOS.

Also known as the Law of the Sea Treaty, the UNCLOS is the international agreement that defined the limits of the territorial seas of nations and the areas in which they could exploit marine resources. It also established the rules for the use of the high seas for international navigation, and outlined the rights and responsibilities of nations in the protection of the marine environment.

The UNCLOS served as a legal basis for the Philippines' case against China before an international tribunal in The Hague. The case was filed in 2013 and won in July 2016, junking China's nine-dash line claim over the South China Sea, but Beijing has been steadfast in refusing to recognize the ruling.
Years of negotiation

As for the DOC, the countries also agreed to practice self-restraint when conducting activities that could escalate disputes or affect stability, including occupying uninhabited islands, reefs and other features.

The DOC stated that the parties concerned reaffirmed "that the adoption of a code of conduct in the South China Sea would further promote peace and stability in the region and agree to work, on the basis of consensus, towards the eventual attainment of this objective."
It is this code that has taken years to negotiate.
According to the ASEAN website, discussions over the COC began in 2018 when the first draft was established. However, the undersigned countries have failed to reach an agreement.
Over the weekend, Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said the COC was about 80% finished, but salient issues remained.
She said the COC is likely to be finished in 2027. The DFA originally wanted to finish it by 2026, which would have coincided with the Philippines' chairship of the ASEAN.
Negotiations and China
While Lazaro did not dive into what the salient issues are, doubts have been raised about China's sincerity in establishing the COC.
The late former foreign affairs secretary Albert del Rosario said in 2014 that he doubted that China would work quickly for a legally binding COC.

"I'm not very optimistic about whether China is serious about an expeditious conclusion [of a Code of Conduct] because I can see the aggressive provocative acts that we are seeing now and which is, I think, is their way to pursue an expansion agenda," Del Rosario said.
The South China Sea, or the West Philippine Sea for areas within Manila's 200-km exclusive economic zone, has been a point of contention between Beijing and Manila for years.
Tensions have considerably risen during President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s term, with the present administration making a stronger claim over its maritime territories. — VDV, GMA News
